get.summary: Stream the events of a Session
get.description: Stream committed Session changes as SSE after a snapshot eventSeq, or Last-Event-ID. Stream reauthorizes each replay/live batch and at intervals no longer than one second while idle; a revocation closes without leaking more events. Events carry bounded projections/invalidation, not full content. Each id is a committed monotonically increasing event sequence; replay gaps/queue overflow send resync-required and close rather than skipping events. Heartbeats about 15 seconds do not advance eventSeq. Clients fetch a new bounded snapshot on a gap.

parameters.name: Last-Event-ID
parameters.description: The sequence of the last Session event the client received (an EventSource sends it on reconnect): the stream replays the events after it. The same cursor as `after`; when both are present they must be equal. Answers `400 SESSION_CURSOR_INVALID` when repeated, not equal to `after`, not a non-negative integer or beyond the latest event. An empty value reads as `0` (replay of every retained event). Without either, the stream starts at the latest event.

200.description: Server-sent events of the Session: `session-change` events whose `id` is the event sequence and whose `data` is the JSON Session event, and `resync-required` when the client must read the Session again. Replay starts after `after` or `Last-Event-ID`; comment lines keep the connection alive.

get.description: Best-effort progress stream for an operation owned by this feature. The stream is not the source of truth: use the operation request and inspection endpoint for outcomes. It starts with a snapshot, then step updates and a terminal completed, failed or recovery-required event; each frame is SSE with event, JSON data and an optional monotonic per-operation id. Each frame has event: snapshot|step|completed|failed|recovery-required, a single JSON data line and id: <monotonic sequence> when available. snapshot contains status and applicable steps; step contains step id and running|done|skipped; completed carries the operation result; failed carries a stable public code only; recovery-required signals operator recovery. The first event is a snapshot, and terminal events close the stream. Unknown steps are ignored by clients. The stream is a display aid, not an authority. A heartbeat comment is sent about every 15 seconds. Runtime keeps terminal events for about 60 seconds, then forgets them. A subscription to an unknown id waits up to 30 seconds, then emits failed/OPERATION_NOT_FOUND (not evidence of a failed operation).
